title: Pedagogy & Outreach
text:
I believe that one of the most profound impacts I can have as a scientist is through instruction and mentorship. I have served as a graduate student instructor for four courses at the University of Michigan: EEB 548 (Population & Community Ecology), EEB 433 (Ornithology), BIO 281 (General Ecology), and BIO 171 (Introduction to Ecology & Evolution). I earned an Outstanding Graduate Instructor Award for my teaching in EEB 548.
I am always seeking to improve my instruction and pedagogy. As a graduate student, I completed a semester-long course on scientific pedagogical practices. In addition, I have worked closely with the University of Michigan Center for Teaching and Learning. I earned a Graduate Teaching Certificate through pursuing additional professional development as an instructor. I also completed the University of Michigan Preparing Future Faculty Program to train in syllabus design and inclusive teaching practices.
Finally, I am passionate about making statistics, data science, and coding accessible to life science students. These are essential skills in the biologist toolkit that nonetheless prove initially intimidating to many students. I have created a syllabus for a course entitled “Spatial and Quantitative Ecology in R” designed to improve statistical reasoning skills for life science students, which I hope to teach in the future.

title: Pedagogy & Outreach
text:
Outreach



One of the great joys of science is the opportunity to make your passions accessible to a variety of audiences. Here’s some of what I’ve been up to recently!

Coverage
Along with my PhD advisor Ben Winger, I partnered with videographers from the University of Michigan Museum of Zoology to create an interactive research kiosk, titled “Data-packed bird backpacks”, explaining the process of tracking birds with geolocators. Check out the videos here!
My geolocation research was also covered by the University of Michigan Biological Station: check it out to learn more about what we learn from tracking songbirds.





Museum-based Education
Natural history museums were my own introduction into the field of ornithology, and made me realize that my lifelong love for birds could turn into an academic pursuit. I have found natural history museums to be a fantastic avenue to reach people of all ages through captivating, close-up looks at the creatures they know and love. As a University of Michigan Museum of Natural History Science Communication Fellow, I’ve had the opportunity to lead behind-the-scenes collections tours, run tabletop displays of museum specimens, and give accessible presentations of museum-based research to families.












Classroom Education
I’ve had lots of fun bringing birds and science to the K-12 classroom. Most recently, I served as a Science Olympiad coach for a team of second graders competing in the “Feathered Friends” division. I’ve also visited the Detroit Public Schools through the Write Like a Scientist Program, along with Dearborn High School as a University of Michigan DNA Day Instructor. Before that, I served as a science mentor in a New Haven magnet school and led first graders on field trips to local saltmarsh habitats. Please feel free to contact me with any opportunities to connect classrooms to science and nature!


Talks
It’s always a treat to chat birds and ornithology with other nature-lovers. Check out some of my recent public talks:

“Tracking Songbird Migration Using Geolocators” (Washtenaw Bird & Nature Alliance)
“Tern Research in the Chesapeake Bay” (Washtenaw Bird & Nature Alliance)

title: Research
text:
I am fascinated by geographic patterns in biodiversity, and the combination of ecological and evolutionary factors that shape the distribution of global biodiversity. Seasonal migration poses an especially rich opportunity to investigate these questions, as the annual movements of migratory animals connect organisms, communities, and ecosystems throughout the world.
My research sits at the intersection of macroecology, community ecology, and animal movement. I explore the ecology and evolution of bird migration across spatial scales, ranging from the movements of individuals to the communities they enter and exit to continental-scale patterns in biodiversity.

title: Research
section: The macroecology and community ecology of seasonal migration
text:
The macroecology and community ecology of seasonal migration
The seasonal influx and exodus of migratory birds profoundly reshapes local communities by altering which species are present. In the process, seasonal migration not only influences community diversity levels, but also introduces new combinations of species interactions. Species are shifting their geographic distributions and phenologies in response to anthropogenic change, generating new communities in the process; it is therefore critical to understand how changes to species interactions and diversity levels affect biological communities.
To better understand the effects of migrants on their communities, I integrate phylogenetic data, community ecology methods, and citizen science datasets to investigate how seasonal migration restructures species interactions. I found that as seasonal migration rearranges the species identities and diversity of bird communities, migrants also affect the factors driving the assembly of these communities. My results show that bird communities can accommodate the arrival of many migratory species in the same family, but this extra diversity also promotes heightened competition among the very closest relatives.



Seasonal migration rearranges biodiversity, and in the process causes a continental-scale redistribution of patterns in phylogenetic dispersion. Hack et al. 2026, Journal of Animal Ecology.

title: Research
section: The migratory geography of annual cycle dynamics
text:
The migratory geography of annual cycle dynamics
The timing of an organism’s annual cycle is governed by its relative investment in reproduction versus survival. While tracking technology has allowed the study of migration at unprecedented detail, we have historically lacked a comparative understanding of how the geography of seasonal migration relates to the pacing of birds’ annual cycles.
To assess the relationships between migratory geography and timing, I have harnessed geolocator tracking data to conduct a comparative assessment of annual cycle pacing in North American songbirds. I’ve attached nearly 200 geolocators to seven species of songbirds breeding in Northern Michigan, and integrated my original field data into a larger dataset curated from published migration tracking studies. I show migration distance to strongly predict the timing and pacing of migratory birds’ annual cycles. My results demonstrate that given the information of the location and duration of a bird’s breeding season, we can predict its migration distance, wintering destination, and overall pacing of its travels. These findings illustrate critical life history tradeoffs in annual cycle allocation.

title: Research
section: Consequences of climate change and urbanization for migratory bird communities
text:
Consequences of climate change and urbanization for migratory bird communities
Patterns of biodiversity and animal movement are likely subject to profound changes under ongoing climate change and urbanization. I am currently designing projects to investigate how geographic patterns in avian biodiversity, community compositions, and seasonal interactions will be affected as climate and land use conditions propagate disruptions to bird communities. Stay tuned for further updates!

title: Matthew Hack
text:
I am an ecologist and ornithologist interested in understanding the ecological and evolutionary processes that shape fundamental patterns of biodiversity and animal movement. I integrate field work, comparative methods, and computational ecology to understand how the movements of seasonal migrants influence their geographic distributions, along with the evolutionary and ecological consequences of differing migratory strategies.
I am currently a PhD candidate in Ecology & Evolutionary Biology at the University of Michigan. Before my graduate work, I earned a B.S. in Ecology & Evolutionary Biology at Yale University, and worked as an Avian Field Technician at the USGS Eastern Ecological Science Center.
